q: One grape is authorised in Alsace for sparkling wine alone, barred from still AOC Alsace. Which is it, and what does that settle at the tasting bench?
accept: chardonnay is permitted only in cremant d'alsace
chardonnay for cremant with still alsace whites being pinot blanc or auxerrois
chardonnay allowed in cremant d'alsace only
ans: Chardonnay — permitted in Crémant d'Alsace only. So a still Alsace white is always some other grape: the broad, low-aromatic white in a flûte is Pinot Blanc or Auxerrois.
exp: Crémant d'Alsace may use Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Riesling and Chardonnay; the rosé is 100% Pinot Noir. The corollary matters more than the rule: 'Pinot Blanc' on an Alsace label is frequently mostly Auxerrois, since the two are legally interchangeable under that name — which is why the variety tastes rounder and lower in acid than Pinot Blanc elsewhere.

q: Alsace 'Muscat' is not one grape. Name the varieties behind it and the practical difference between them.
accept: muscat blanc a petits grains and muscat ottonel
petits grains plus ottonel usually blended
muscat ottonel and muscat blanc a petits grains
petits grains finer ottonel earlier and unreliable
ans: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (with its Rose mutation) and Muscat Ottonel. Petits Grains is the finer and later-ripening, with grapey intensity and better acidity; Ottonel ripens earlier and gives a softer, more floral, less piercing wine but sets fruit unreliably. Most Alsace Muscat is a blend of the two.
exp: Muscat of Alexandria is not permitted — it is the standard wrong answer, imported from the south of France. Muscat is the smallest of the four noble varieties in Alsace at roughly 2% of plantings, is almost always made dry, and is the region's classic asparagus wine. Ottonel's poor set is why the variety keeps shrinking: growers will not keep a vine that fails in a cold flowering.

q: Alsace runs through two departments. Which holds the large majority of the grands crus, and how does the other differ?
accept: haut-rhin holds most of the grand crus bas-rhin is cooler
haut rhin around colmar has the majority bas rhin north is leaner
haut-rhin south majority of crus bas-rhin cooler and lighter
haut-rhin has thirty-seven of the fifty-one crus and bas-rhin the other fourteen
ans: The Haut-Rhin, in the south around Colmar, holds 37 of the 51 grands crus - roughly three-quarters, and most of the celebrated names: Rangen, Schlossberg, Brand, Hengst, Goldert, Rosacker. The Bas-Rhin to the north is cooler and later-ripening, giving leaner, higher-acid, more delicate wines, and holds the other fourteen - Kastelberg, Muenchberg, Wiebelsberg, Moenchberg and Zotzenberg among them, none of which is a minor site.
exp: The Vosges are at their highest opposite the Haut-Rhin, so the rain shadow is deepest there - Colmar's dryness and sunshine are a Haut-Rhin advantage that the Bas-Rhin does not fully share. The northern crus are also where the odder soils and relics sit: Kastelberg on Steige schist, Muenchberg on sandstone with volcanic deposits, Klevener de Heiligenstein's Savagnin Rose, and the Pinot Noir of Ottrott. Warming has been kinder to the Bas-Rhin than to anywhere else in the region.

q: Australia's GI system differs from the AOC model in that it regulates:
ans: Boundaries only — no variety, yield or method rules (85% origin/variety/vintage labeling)
exp: Style is the market's business, not the law's.

q: The GI 'South Eastern Australia', printed on much of the country's export volume, covers what?
accept: multi-state zone of nsw victoria tasmania south australia and queensland
super zone covering the whole east including tasmania
blending gi spanning new south wales victoria tasmania and south australia
most of the country east of the western australian border
ans: A multi-state super-zone taking in all of New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania plus the grape-growing parts of South Australia and Queensland — a blending licence rather than a place
exp: Because Australian GIs regulate boundaries and nothing else, a perfectly legal GI can span half a continent. It exists so Riverland, Riverina and Murray Darling fruit can be blended freely, and it is the proof that 'GI' on an Australian label promises far less specificity than an AOP does.
